# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

The Comment splits into two parts of very different quality.

- **Sections 1–5** are a strong, data-based re-analysis. They confirm, with microdata, most of the concerns I raised about the Halden pilot: scheduled versus actual hours, unadjusted revenue, the near-mechanical per-hour gain, retail output falling, and decaying energy. They also add a serious new finding on attrition.
- **Sections 6–8** draw a conclusion ("entirely an artifact") that the authors' own numbers do not support. That section relies on an arithmetic slip, mischaracterises the Varden trial, and applies evidential standards selectively.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Paper | Recomputed | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Table 2, as reported | +23.4% | 98.7/0.800 = 123.4 | ✓ |
| Record-based, scheduled hours | +18.9% | 95.1/0.800 = 118.9 | ✓ |
| Manager-reported, actual hours | +14.6% | 98.4/0.859 = 114.6 | ✓ |
| Record-based, actual hours | +10.8% | 95.4/0.861 = 110.8 | ✓ |
| Hours, 27 organisations | −14.1% | 34.6/40.3 = 0.859 | ✓ |
| Hours, 17 organisations | −13.9% | 34.8/40.4 = 0.861 | ✓ |
| Real revenue | ≈ −2.6% | 1.014/1.041 = 0.974 | ✓ |
| Hours decomposition (§3) | 34.6 h/week | 32 + 4×0.7 + 1.6 = **36.4** | ✗ |
| Energy returns to baseline | "around month ten" | Linear extrapolation gives **≈ month 8.7** | ✗ |

**The hours decomposition doesn't reconcile.** An extra 0.7 hours on each of four days, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, adds 4.4 hours to a 32-hour schedule, which gives about 36.4 hours. The reported figure is 34.6. Either a component is wrong, or the components are averaged over different organisations or periods. This matters because the 0.859 hours ratio drives two of the four rows in Table 2.

**The energy extrapolation is off.** Energy fell by 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6, so the remaining 0.29 SD would be gone in about 2.7 more months, at roughly month 8.7. This doesn't change the argument, but it should be corrected.

---

## Strengths

**1. The attrition finding is the most important new fact.** The working paper says the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata show that seven of the nine left after the reduced schedule had begun, and six gave workload or output as the main reason. If accurate, this is a material misdescription in the original paper, not just a limitation. Halden should be asked to respond directly.

**2. The manager-versus-records comparison is persuasive evidence of a systematic gap.** The manager index was higher in 19 of 23 organisations, which would be very unlikely by chance (sign test p ≈ 0.003). The Comment rightly avoids any suggestion of bad faith.

**3. The actual-hours correction is the right one**, and the resulting gap (14% fall rather than 20%) closely matches the Varden timesheets (13% and 17%). That cross-study consistency is reassuring.

**4. Sections 4 and 5 are correct.** Real revenue fell. The sector-generality claim is an artefact of dividing by 0.8. The Data note candidly says that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

---

## Problems

### 1. The abstract claims a correction the paper never makes

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output and hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never corrected: the 17 organisations are still survivors, as Section 6 itself says.

The authors could bound the attrition effect, either with worst-case or Lee-type bounds, or with an intention-to-treat calculation that assigns plausible outcomes to the nine withdrawals. Otherwise the abstract should be corrected.

### 2. Table 2 mixes samples

Each row uses a different subset: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The "successive corrections" therefore combine the effect of each correction with changes in which organisations are included. All four specifications should be shown on the same 17 organisations. That would isolate how much of the fall from 23.4% is due to the output correction and how much to the hours correction.

### 3. "Record-based" output is not automatically the truth

Treating submitted records as the benchmark is reasonable but not neutral:

- **Billable hours delivered** is listed as an output record. In a professional-services firm it is largely an input measure, so it falls almost mechanically when hours fall, even if value per hour rises (for example, on fixed-fee work). Using it biases the record-based index downward.
- Records may capture only part of an organisation's output. A manager's index might legitimately reflect quality or work the records omit.

The 19-of-23 pattern still strongly suggests manager optimism. But the authors should report the gap by type of record, and check whether it persists when organisations using billable hours are excluded.

### 4. The novelty argument is not tested, although the data to test it exist

The Comment infers a novelty effect in *productivity* from a decline in self-reported *energy*. Energy is not output. Even on their reading, energy was still 0.29 SD above baseline at month six. Extrapolating a straight line through two survey points is also weak; the pattern could equally be a rise followed by a plateau.

Crucially, the Halden output index was collected **monthly**, so the microdata contain an output time series. If novelty were driving the gain, record-based output per actual hour should decline from month 3 to month 6. The authors should show that trajectory. Without it, Section 6 is conjecture, and "the burden of proof" language substitutes for an analysis they could have done.

### 5. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own numbers and the Varden trial

After corrections, a gain of about 11% remains. The authors attribute all of it to novelty without direct evidence (point 4). It is fair to say the residual is probably smaller than 10.8%: attrition is uncorrected, and some day-off work is unlogged. But "entirely an artifact" does not follow.

The Comment also uses the Varden trial selectively:

- It calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature".
- The same trial's case-processing stratum, with the same randomised design, administrative output, timesheet hours and nine months' duration, found output per actual hour **+12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**.
- That design removes exactly the selection and measurement problems the Comment identifies. Of the three explanations the Comment offers (measurement, selection and novelty), only novelty remains possible.
- Even the counter stratum showed +6.7% per hour, although, as I noted earlier, that is plausibly a queue-utilisation effect.

A fair conclusion from the combined evidence would be:

> The Halden figure substantially overstates the per-hour gain. A smaller gain in backlog-based work survives randomisation and objective measurement over nine months. Coverage-bound work loses output. Durability is unresolved.

### 6. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis

- **The offices weren't "selected after the results were known".** The seven offices are the entire treated case-processing stratum, defined by stratification before randomisation. What was unregistered was collecting meeting data. The Varden authors say so, and the Comment is right that the analysis is weak evidence.
- **Varden didn't present it as a mechanism.** The authors explicitly said it "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test. The Comment's instruction that it "should not be cited as a mechanism" argues against a claim nobody made.
- **The Comment ignores corroboration in its own data source.** Halden's manager interviews report meeting cuts in 47 of 58 organisations.
- **The meetings hypothesis is not an artefact explanation.** It implies a real gain per hour that comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest. The Comment's own scepticism could use this. As I noted on Varden, if treated offices started with about 7 hours of meetings, the gain per hour of non-meeting work may be only about 3%. That would imply the benefit might be had without cutting hours at all. The Comment treats "not caused by rest" as if it meant "not real".

### 7. Inconsistent evidential standards

The Comment rejects a correlation across 7 offices as the kind of finding that "does not replicate". Yet it relies on:

- a record-based retail figure from **3** organisations (−11.2%), and
- Varden's counter stratum of **5 v 5** offices, which is not corrected for small numbers of clusters, as I noted in the Varden review.

These may well be right, and are consistent with each other. But the same scepticism should apply to all three findings.

### 8. Generalisation beyond the data

The conclusion extends from one pilot to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general. A re-analysis of one uncontrolled pilot cannot support a claim about all schemes, especially when the only randomised evidence it cites partly points the other way.

---

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the abstract: attrition is identified, not corrected. Add bounds for the attrition effect if possible.
2. Show all Table 2 specifications on the common 17-organisation subset, with intervals.
3. Reconcile the hours decomposition in Section 3.
4. Report the manager–record gap by record type, and drop billable-hours organisations as a sensitivity check.
5. Test novelty directly using the monthly output series, and correct the energy extrapolation.
6. Engage with Varden's case-processing result and rewrite Section 7 to describe the meetings analysis accurately.
7. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion proportionate to the residual estimate.

**Overall:** Sections 1–5 should substantially change how the Halden pilot is read. The attrition misdescription in particular warrants a formal response from the Halden authors. The headline conclusion, however, does not follow from those sections. Their own corrected estimate and the strongest available trial both indicate a smaller but non-zero per-hour gain in non-coverage work, with durability still open. If you're synthesising across the three papers, I can draft a short summary of where the evidence now stands.
